author: D. S. Harrison
title: Wisconsin health officials urge residents to get vaccinated against respiratory viruses this fall
text:
Secretary-designee Kirsten Johnson | Wisconsin Health Care Association Website
Secretary-designee Kirsten Johnson | Wisconsin Health Care Association Website
The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) is urging residents to get vaccinated against respiratory viruses as the fall season approaches. Updated vaccines for flu and COVID-19 are now becoming widely available across the state for the 2025-26 respiratory virus season. These vaccines are designed to protect against the current strains circulating this year. RSV vaccines and antibodies are also available for eligible groups, including most older adults, pregnant people, and infants.
"Fall is the time of year when we start to see respiratory virus activity increase, and getting vaccinated now gives you the best protection ahead of the season," said Paula Tran, state health officer and Division of Public Health administrator. "Vaccines are one of the most effective ways to protect our health because they boost our immune system's ability to recognize and fight illnesses. This helps reduce your chance of getting seriously ill."
Respiratory viruses tend to increase during Wisconsin’s fall and winter months, though they circulate year-round. During the 2024-25 season, nearly 7,000 people in Wisconsin were hospitalized due to complications from seasonal flu, marking it as one of the most severe influenza seasons in the past decade.
DHS recommends that everyone receive seasonal vaccines for flu, COVID-19, and RSV. All recommended vaccines for the fall have undergone thorough review and ongoing monitoring for safety and effectiveness.
Residents are encouraged to talk with their health care providers about personal health risks and the best prevention steps for themselves and their families.
Flu vaccines are updated each year to match circulating strains, and annual vaccination is recommended for everyone aged 6 months and older. This is particularly important for high-risk groups such as older adults, those with chronic conditions, pregnant people, young children, and individuals who interact with these populations.
COVID-19 vaccines are also updated annually to address new variants. DHS recommends that all Wisconsinites 6 months and older receive the updated COVID-19 vaccine. The recommendation is especially emphasized for those over 65, individuals who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine, people at risk of severe complications (including infants, young children, pregnant or recently pregnant individuals), and anyone spending time with these groups. People who have recently had a COVID-19 infection should wait three months before getting vaccinated.
The RSV vaccine is not needed every year; instead, a one-time dose is advised for adults over 50 at increased risk of severe disease and for all people aged 75 and older. Pregnant people between 32 and 36 weeks gestation from September through January should receive one dose to help protect infants at highest risk of severe RSV illness. If this dose is not given during pregnancy, an RSV antibody shot is recommended for infants under eight months old and some toddlers during RSV season (October-March). The RSV vaccine can be administered alongside other vaccines.
Vaccine appointments are available through healthcare providers, clinics, and pharmacies as supplies arrive. Residents can contact their primary care provider or local health department to schedule an appointment. For those without insurance or whose insurance does not cover vaccines, programs like Vaccines for Children and Vaccines for Adults may provide assistance.
Other recommended preventive measures include regular handwashing with soap and water, disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, and wearing N95 or KN95 masks when traveling or in crowded spaces.
DHS continues its year-round monitoring of vaccination rates and respiratory virus activity statewide through data reported by healthcare providers and laboratories. Information on respiratory activity as well as immunization dashboards for COVID-19, flu, and RSV in Wisconsin residents is available on DHS data webpages.
